opus-5.5.text:
I think the most interesting question for anyone building a coding-agent startup right now is: what do you build that doesn't get eaten by the next model release?

Every few months the underlying models get meaningfully better, and a lot of the scaffolding people spent months building just stops being necessary. Elaborate prompt chains, custom retry logic, clever ways of chunking a codebase so the model doesn't lose track. A lot of that was compensating for model weaknesses, and when the weakness goes away, so does the moat. So the question I keep coming back to is: which parts of your product get *better* as the model gets better, and which parts become obsolete?

My rough heuristic is that you want to be building the things that sit around the model rather than patching over it. Things like the environment the agent runs in, how it gets feedback, how it runs tests, how it understands whether it actually succeeded. And the interface for a human to review, steer, and trust what the agent did. Those don't go away when the model gets smarter. If anything they matter more, because now the agent is attempting bigger, longer tasks, and verification and oversight become the bottleneck.

The related question I find fascinating is where the human sits in the loop. Right now a lot of products assume a developer watching an agent in their IDE, approving each step. But as agents get more reliable, the unit of work shifts from "help me write this function" to "go close this ticket" or "go do this migration across fifty repos." That's a really different product. It's closer to managing a team than using a tool. I don't think anyone has fully figured out what the right interface for that looks like, and I think whoever does is going to be in a really strong position.

So, build for where the models are going rather than where they are today, and focus on the parts that compound with model improvements instead of competing with them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building products that improve with model releases and how agents should fit into workflows, but it does not raise a question about coding-agent benchmarks diverging from real customer needs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The question I keep coming back to is: what happens to your product when the model gets dramatically better in six months?

A lot of coding-agent startups right now are building elaborate scaffolding around the model, with careful prompt chains, retrieval pipelines, and hand-tuned heuristics for when to search or when to edit a file. That scaffolding is doing real work today, and it is often the reason the product feels good. But most of it exists to compensate for things the model can't yet do on its own. Every time a new model ships, some chunk of that scaffolding becomes dead weight, or worse, it actively gets in the way because it's constraining a model that would have made a better decision unassisted.

So the interesting strategic question is, which parts of what you're building are durable, and which parts are a bet against model progress? Durable things tend to look like: integration with the places developers actually work, trust and permission systems, good feedback loops so the agent can verify its own work, and the accumulated context about a specific codebase or team. Those get more valuable as models improve, not less.

The teams I find most interesting are the ones who are honest with themselves about that split. They ask, if the model were twice as capable, would I delete this code or keep it? And they try to make the things they keep as simple as possible, because simplicity is what lets you ride the improvement curve instead of fighting it.

r001.rationale: The response asks how coding-agent products should adapt as models improve and which product components are durable. It does not discuss benchmarks or how they diverge from what real customers want.

astra-6.text: The question I find most interesting is: what does software development look like when the agent is doing most of the coding? Are you building a better tool for a developer who’s still driving every step, or are you letting them delegate an entire task and come back to review the result? Those lead to very different products. And for a startup, the challenge is figuring out what stays valuable as the underlying models get better.

sol-6.1.text:
The question I find most interesting is: as the models get better, does your product get more valuable, or does the model just absorb what you do? For coding agents, that’s a pretty fundamental question. You can spend a lot of time getting an agent to work around a limitation, and then the next model comes out and that limitation disappears.

So I’m interested in what you build that compounds with model progress. Is it understanding the company’s codebase? Is it the feedback loop from running tests and seeing what actually works? Is it how the agent fits into the team’s workflow? Ideally, a better model lets you take on a much bigger piece of the problem for the customer.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a coding-agent product gains value as models improve, but it does not discuss how benchmarks diverge from what real customers want.
